content: 1. Collaboration with the WHO country office is essential when planning the closure of a site. The rationale and timeline for the proposed closure must be clearly outlined. 2. Countries may seek advice from the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) on an ad hoc basis, and the GPEI will provide recommendations within one week. 3. Any site opened in response to an outbreak should be closed in consultation with the lead of the outbreak response. 4. Before informing stakeholders of a site closure decision, the WHO country office, regional office, and headquarters may hold a final discussion. The decision should then be communicated through a summary report. 5. When closing a site, the regional office must be informed, and the site data form (electronic or paper-based) should be updated to reflect the new status in the environmental site database. Sample Collection, Packaging, and Transport 6. Grab sampling is the WHO-recommended method for poliovirus surveillance. A 1-liter wastewater sample is collected at a predetermined date and time, as specified in the site schedule, while adhering to biosafety measures. 7. An alternative method, accepted by WHO and used in several countries, involves collecting samples via a bag-mediated filtration system. 8. Field personnel must be adequately equipped, trained, and supervised in a supportive environment to ensure efficient sample collection. 9. Samples must be packaged to prevent contamination and preserve live enteroviruses for laboratory testing. 10. Samples should be transported in robust, dedicated containers using the triple packing system for biological products or diagnostic specimens. 11. Samples must arrive at the laboratory intact, without signs of toxicity or bacterial overgrowth, and with all enteroviruses preserved for testing. 12. Samples should reach the laboratory within three days of collection for national shipments or within seven days for international shipments. 13. If same-day shipping is not possible, facilities with cold storage capacity, such as national laboratories or WHO country offices, should act as intermediary depots. Samples should be refrigerated at 4°C (range: 2–8°C). 14. If shipping is delayed, samples should be stored in a freezer at -20°C and shipped frozen. 15. Sewage samples must not be stored in the same refrigerator as clinical samples for acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) or other diseases due to the high risk of contamination. Environmental Surveillance Supervision 16. Given the complexity of sewage sampling and its impact on subsequent procedures, all activities—from sampling to the arrival of samples at the polio laboratory—must adhere to high-quality standards. 17. National programs should ensure that at least 80% of sample collections at each site undergo on-site supervision on a quarterly basis, and this should be documented. 18. A monitoring tool is available to evaluate the performance of sampling sites. Data Collection and Management 19. Several forms are available to facilitate the identification and registration of environmental sites and assist with the collection and sharing of sample data and results. 20. Each environmental sample must carry a unique identification code beginning with ENV to denote it as an environmental sample, followed by codes designating the geographical location and site. 21. Laboratory results for environmental samples must be reported by polio-accredited laboratories and uploaded to the database immediately after they are obtained. 22. Laboratories must share results with national programs in a timely and comprehensive manner and assist in interpreting the findings and their significance. Performance Indicators for Environmental Surveillance 23. The sensitivity of the network is measured by the proportion of samples positive for enterovirus (polio or non-polio enterovirus), with a target of >50%. 24. Timeliness of sample collection is assessed by the proportion of samples collected on the scheduled day and at the scheduled time, with a target of >80%. 25. The adequacy of samples is determined by the proportion of samples arriving at a WHO-accredited laboratory in good condition, with a target of >80%. 26. Timeliness of sample shipment is measured by the proportion of samples arriving at the laboratory within three days (national) or seven days (international) of collection, with a target of >80%. 27. Timeliness of laboratory reporting is assessed by the proportion of samples for which results are sent to submitting laboratories/agencies within a defined period, with a target of >80%. Site Evaluation and Corrective Actions 28. The performance of a country’s environmental surveillance system should be periodically evaluated and integrated with AFP surveillance reviews when possible. 29. If enterovirus isolation is <50% and no poliovirus is detected, on-site assessments should be conducted, all data evaluated, and the site either discontinued or subjected to a second six-month sampling period. 30. If enterovirus isolation is <50% and poliovirus is detected, collection should continue for an additional six months, and the decision to continue or close the site must be made at 12 months. Programmatic Response to WPV or VDPV Detection 31. When wild poliovirus (WPV) or vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) is detected in the environment, follow-up investigations must determine the significance of the findings. 32. The response to WPV or VDPV detection should align with global standard operating procedures (SOPs) and the national outbreak response plan. 33. In polio-free countries, the detection of WPV or VDPV represents a public health emergency requiring immediate investigation. 34. Rapid communication of suspected outbreaks is critical, with all reporting units notified within 24 hours and WHO informed within 48 hours. 35. Enhanced environmental sampling and active case searches should be conducted to determine if an outbreak is occurring. 36. Immunization coverage should be reviewed to assess the likelihood of susceptible populations sustaining poliovirus transmission. 37. Virological investigations, including genome characterization of WPV or VDPV isolates, should be expedited to assist in identifying possible sources and transmission chains.
